item.text:
**Bottom Line**  
2024 looks mostly negative on 5B.8. There were real pro-equity moves in education and social spending, especially around primary schooling and girls’ access, but the stronger evidence says the gains were not broadly or fairly shared: social protection stayed tiny, social infrastructure remained weak, conflict areas were left behind, and mining/resource gains were associated with evictions and underfunded services. I found no direct 2024 source that actually audited whether budget gains were steered toward regime supporters, so that part remains an evidence gap.

- **Strengthening Public Social Spending in DRC** — IMF, 2024-07-15, https://www.elibrary.imf.org/view/journals/002/2024/227/article-A002-en.xml; Claim: social spending rose and education/health were prioritized, with free primary education expanding access, but social protection remained minimal and much of the budget was still absorbed by salaries and current spending. This is a limited pro-equity signal, but it also shows weak depth of redistribution. IDs: `5B.8`, `5B.6`
- **Democratic Republic of Congo: Expanding and Equipping Primary School Classrooms for Better Learning Outcomes** — World Bank, 2024-02-26, https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2024/02/28/democratic-republic-of-congo-afe-expanding-and-equipping-primary-school-classrooms-for-better-learning-outcomes; Claim: the new education project was explicitly framed around equitable access in the provinces, including girls and students with disabilities, plus merit-based teacher recruitment and decentralized planning. This is one of the clearest positive inclusion signals. IDs: `5B.8`, `5B.6`
- **Prioritizing human capital: lessons from the Democratic Republic of Congo** — World Bank, 2024-03-28, https://blogs.worldbank.org/en/investinpeople/prioritizing-human-capital--lessons-from-the-democratic-republic; Claim: armed conflict in the eastern provinces was reducing access to housing, health, education, and basic needs, implying that economic gains were not being distributed evenly across regions. IDs: `5B.8`, `5B.6`
- **DRC: President Tshisekedi must use second term to tackle human rights crisis** — Amnesty International, 2024-06-24, https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2024/06/drc-president-tshisekedi-must-use-second-term-to-tackle-human-rights-crisis/; Claim: Amnesty said public resources were being squandered, essential services were underfunded, and mining expansion was producing forced evictions and pollution. That is strong evidence against broad, fair sharing of gains. IDs: `5B.8`, `5B.6`
- **Strengthening Public Social Spending in DRC** — IMF, 2024-07-15, https://www.elibrary.imf.org/view/journals/002/2024/227/article-A002-en.xml; Claim: the IMF said efforts to reduce inequalities were still insufficient, budget credibility was weak, and deficits in social infrastructure persisted. This is strong counterevidence to a claim of fair distribution. IDs: `5B.8`, `5B.6`
- **Congo election commission overspent, awarded opaque contracts: report** — Reuters, 2024-01-15, https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/congo-election-commission-overspent-awarded-opaque-contracts-report-2024-01-15/; Claim: the election commission could not account for about $400 million and used opaque procurement. This is indirect but concrete evidence of non-transparent resource handling rather than neutral distribution. IDs: `5B.8`, `5B.5`
- **Democratic Republic of Congo: Expanding and Equipping Primary School Classrooms for Better Learning Outcomes** — World Bank, 2024-02-26, https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2024/02/28/democratic-republic-of-congo-afe-expanding-and-equipping-primary-school-classrooms-for-better-learning-outcomes; Claim: school leaders in Kinshasa and the provinces reported overcrowded classrooms, missing learning materials, weak staffing, and poor water/sanitation, showing the benefits of public spending were still not reaching people evenly. IDs: `5B.8`, `5B.6`

**Search Gap**  
I did not find a 2024 source that directly measured provincial budget shares, class-based transfers, or patronage-linked economic distribution under Tshisekedi. The evidence is therefore indirect: social spending composition, education/health delivery, mining-related displacement, and conflict-zone service gaps.
